---
title: "Crashes, Drawdowns & Nameable Events"
subtitle: "Putting dates and names on the left tail"
---



A **crash** is not a special object in the data — it is simply a day deep in the
**left tail**.  The previous page showed those tails are fat; this page walks over
to them and reads the dates.  It turns out the worst days have names you'll
recognise.

---

## 1 · The Worst Days Have Names

Average the five banks into one series and ask for its worst days.  They bunch
into two episodes — the **2008–09 financial crisis** and the **March-2020 COVID
crash**:

::: {#408350d3 .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
bank_avg = R[BANKS].mean(axis=1)
worst = bank_avg.sort_values().head(5)
print("five worst average-bank days:")
for d, v in worst.items():
    print(f"  {d.date()}   {v:+.1%}")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
five worst average-bank days:
  2009-01-20   -25.6%
  2008-12-01   -21.4%
  2009-02-27   -19.7%
  2020-03-16   -16.7%
  2009-04-20   -16.6%
```
:::
:::


But deep left-tail days are not confined to those two windows.  Nameable crashes
recur across the whole period — each tied to a vote, a downgrade, a pandemic, a
policy shock — and the figure marks five of them, well spread across nineteen
years.

::: {#cell-fig-events .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
events = {
    pd.Timestamp("2008-09-15"): "Lehman",
    pd.Timestamp("2011-08-08"): "US downgrade",
    pd.Timestamp("2016-06-24"): "Brexit",
    pd.Timestamp("2020-03-16"): "COVID crash",
    pd.Timestamp("2025-04-03"): "Tariff crash",
}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.2, 4.4))
ax.plot(bank_avg.index, bank_avg, color=COOL, lw=0.6)
ax.axhline(0, color=INK, lw=0.7)
for i, (d, name) in enumerate(events.items()):
    mark_event(ax, d, name, top=0.97 - 0.12 * (i % 2))   # stagger bubbles
ax.set_ylabel("average bank daily return"); ax.set_xlabel("date")
ax.set_title("The left tail, with names attached", fontsize=12)
despine(ax); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}

The very deepest days of all sit in the dense 2008–09 cluster on the left.](03-crashes-and-drawdowns_files/figure-html/fig-events-output-1.png){#fig-events width=1088 height=513}

The five marked events, with sources:

- **Lehman Brothers' bankruptcy** — 2008-09-15 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bankruptcy_of_Lehman_Brothers))
- **Black Monday 2011**, after S&P's US credit-rating downgrade — 2011-08-08 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Monday_%282011%29))
- **Brexit referendum result** — 2016-06-24 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_Kingdom_European_Union_membership_referendum))
- **COVID-19 crash** — 2020-03-16 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_stock_market_crash))
- **"Liberation Day" tariff crash** — 2025-04-03 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_stock_market_crash))

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## A Crash Is a Quantile, Not a Category
There is no switch in the data that flips to "crash."  We *define* one — say, a day
below the 5th percentile — and the definition is a dial.  Keep that in mind on the
next page, where the same dial moves a co-crash headline from 3% to 67%.
:::

To make the dial concrete, *turn it*.  Pick a percentile, read the **cutoff return**
off the distribution, and everything at or below it is a crash day.  Below we do this
for the bank-average and for a single name (JPM), and we print the cutoff, the count of
flagged days, and the first few flagged dates — the boolean mask that the definition
produces:

::: {#0e44463e .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
# the dial: a percentile q -> a cutoff return -> a boolean crash mask
q = 0.05                                       # 5th-percentile definition of "crash"
cut_avg = bank_avg.quantile(q)                 # cutoff return for the bank-average
mask_avg = bank_avg <= cut_avg                 # boolean: True on crash days
print(f"bank-average  q={q:.0%}  cutoff = {cut_avg:+.2%}   "
      f"{mask_avg.sum()} crash days of {len(mask_avg)} "
      f"({mask_avg.mean():.1%} of the sample)")

cut_jpm = R["JPM"].quantile(q)                 # same dial, one name
mask_jpm = R["JPM"] <= cut_jpm
print(f"JPM           q={q:.0%}  cutoff = {cut_jpm:+.2%}   "
      f"{mask_jpm.sum()} crash days")

print("\nfirst five flagged bank-average dates:")
for d in bank_avg.index[mask_avg][:5]:
    print(f"  {d.date()}   {bank_avg[d]:+.2%}")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
bank-average  q=5%  cutoff = -3.21%   239 crash days of 4778 (5.0% of the sample)
JPM           q=5%  cutoff = -3.17%   239 crash days

first five flagged bank-average dates:
  2007-02-27   -4.70%
  2007-08-03   -3.22%
  2007-08-09   -4.32%
  2007-11-01   -5.48%
  2007-11-07   -4.86%
```
:::
:::


Now **move the dial** and watch the count respond.  A looser threshold (10%) admits
roughly twice as many days as a tighter one (5%) — there is nothing magical about
either number, only a choice about how deep into the tail "crash" begins:

::: {#9c533197 .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code}
print("threshold sensitivity (bank-average):")
for q in (0.01, 0.05, 0.10):
    cut = bank_avg.quantile(q)
    n = int((bank_avg <= cut).sum())
    print(f"  q={q:>4.0%}   cutoff = {cut:+.2%}   {n:>3d} crash days")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
threshold sensitivity (bank-average):
  q=  1%   cutoff = -6.72%    48 crash days
  q=  5%   cutoff = -3.21%   239 crash days
  q= 10%   cutoff = -2.10%   478 crash days
```
:::
:::


The cutoff softens and the day-count swells as `q` grows — the same series, three
different "crashes."  That is the whole point: the category is manufactured by the
quantile, so whoever sets `q` sets the headline.

## 2 · Drawdown: the Pain of Staying Invested

A single bad day is one thing; the **drawdown** is the cumulative wound — how far
below its previous peak an investment has fallen, and *for how long*.  Reconstruct
JPM's equity curve and shade the **underwater** region between the running peak and
the price.  The depth is brutal — but the recovery is the real point, and not every
bank got one.

::: {#cell-fig-drawdown .cell execution_count=6}
``` {.python .cell-code}
eq = 100 * np.exp(R["JPM"].cumsum())
peak = eq.cummax()
dd = eq / peak - 1.0
trough = dd.idxmin()
eq_c = 100 * np.exp(R["C"].cumsum())          # Citigroup, for contrast
dd_c = eq_c / eq_c.cummax() - 1.0

fig, (axT, axB) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(9.2, 5.4), sharex=True,
                               height_ratios=[2, 1])
axT.plot(eq.index, eq, color=COOL, lw=1.2, label="JPM (indexed to 100)")
axT.plot(peak.index, peak, color=INK, lw=0.9, ls="--", label="running peak")
axT.set_ylabel("price"); axT.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False, loc="upper left")
axT.set_title("Equity curve and its drawdown", fontsize=12); despine(axT)

axB.fill_between(dd.index, dd * 100, 0, color=CRASH, alpha=0.30)
axB.plot(dd_c.index, dd_c * 100, color=INK, lw=1.0)
axB.axvline(trough, color=INK, lw=0.8, ls=":")
# label the two curves inline, in the calm 2013–16 gap, to avoid a box on the line
axB.text(pd.Timestamp("2014-06-01"), -16, "JPM", color=CRASH,
         fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")
axB.text(pd.Timestamp("2014-06-01"), -72, "Citigroup", color=INK,
         fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")
axB.annotate(f"JPM max drawdown {dd.min():.0%}\n{trough.date()}",
             (trough, dd.min() * 100), textcoords="offset points",
             xytext=(12, 12), fontsize=9, color=INK)
axB.set_ylabel("drawdown (%)"); axB.set_xlabel("date"); despine(axB)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Top: JPM equity curve (indexed to 100) with its running peak. Bottom: the drawdown — percent below the prior peak. JPM's worst, −68%, bottoms on 2009-03-09 in the depths of the crisis, then claws back to new highs by 2013 (the shaded region returns to zero). Citigroup's drawdown (dark line) is the other story: −98% at the trough, and nineteen years later still some −69% below its 2007 peak — a wound that never healed.](03-crashes-and-drawdowns_files/figure-html/fig-drawdown-output-1.png){#fig-drawdown width=1089 height=633}
:::
:::


Drawdown has two dimensions — **depth** and **duration**.  JPM's was deep but
temporary.  Citigroup's was near-total and, after the dilution and a 1-for-10
reverse split that the crisis forced, effectively permanent: an investor who held
from 2007 has still not seen their money back.  Same sector, same crash, opposite
endings.

## 3 · The Same Days, Seen in the Distribution

Crashes and the histogram are two views of one thing.  Mark the worst days back on
the return distribution and they land exactly where the **left tail** is shaded —
the fat tail of the last page is *made of* these named days.

::: {#cell-fig-tail-marks .cell execution_count=7}
``` {.python .cell-code}
x = bank_avg.to_numpy()
cut = np.quantile(x, 0.05)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.8, 4.2))
bins = np.arange(x.min() - 0.003, 0.0, 0.004)   # 0.4%-wide bins resolve the tail
ax.hist(x, bins=bins, color=BAND, alpha=0.85)
ax.axvspan(x.min() - 0.01, cut, color=CRASH, alpha=0.15, label="worst 5% of days")
for d, name in events.items():
    xpos = bank_avg[d]
    ax.axvline(xpos, color=CRASH, lw=1.0, ls="--")
    ax.annotate(name, (xpos, 26), ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=8,
                color=CRASH, rotation=90)
ax.set_xlim(x.min() - 0.01, -0.02)              # zoom: just the left tail
ax.set_ylim(0, 55)
ax.set_xlabel("average bank daily return"); ax.set_ylabel("days")
ax.set_title("Inside the worst 5%: the named crashes have company", fontsize=12)
ax.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False, loc="upper left"); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Zoomed into the left tail — the bulk of days sits off the right edge, near zero. Bars count how many days landed at each return; the worst 5% (below −3.2%) are shaded. The five named crashes (dashed, labelled) each fall among real, if rare, tail days. They are residents of the fat tail, not outliers off the chart.](03-crashes-and-drawdowns_files/figure-html/fig-tail-marks-output-1.png){#fig-tail-marks width=1041 height=489}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip}
## The Takeaway
"Crash" = deep left-tail day; "drawdown" = cumulative distance below the peak.
Both are everyday consequences of fat tails — and on the next page we'll see the
banks don't take these days *alone*.
:::

---

## What the Labs Reload From Here

This chapter is where the **crash-day mask** is born, and several dependence labs
*reload* it rather than re-deriving it.  The reason is on the next page: dependence
behaves differently on crash days than on calm days — the distance-correlation−Spearman
gap widens, and tail co-crash spikes — so those labs need to split the sample on
exactly the mask we define here.  The recipe is one line of loading and three of
masking; copy it as-is:

::: {#cell-fig-reload-mask .cell execution_count=8}
``` {.python .cell-code}
# --- the recipe the labs reload (one loader call, then the dial) ---
R = datasets.load_returns()                              # prepared panel
bank_avg = R[["JPM", "BAC", "C", "WFC", "GS"]].mean(axis=1)   # the five banks
crash = bank_avg <= bank_avg.quantile(0.10)              # bank-average crash mask
crash_jpm = R["JPM"] <= R["JPM"].quantile(0.10)          # per-name version (JPM)

# --- display it, so the reader sees exactly what the labs will eat ---
cut = bank_avg.quantile(0.10)
print(f"crash mask  q=10%  cutoff = {cut:+.2%}")
print(f"  bank-average : {crash.sum():>3d} crash days "
      f"({crash.mean():.1%} of {len(crash)} days)")
print(f"  JPM          : {crash_jpm.sum():>3d} crash days "
      f"({crash_jpm.mean():.1%})")
print("\nfirst five flagged (bank-average) dates:")
for d in bank_avg.index[crash][:5]:
    print(f"  {d.date()}   {bank_avg[d]:+.2%}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.2, 3.8))
ax.plot(bank_avg.index, bank_avg, color=COOL, lw=0.6, zorder=1)
ax.scatter(bank_avg.index[crash], bank_avg[crash], s=10, color=CRASH,
           zorder=2, label="crash days (≤ 10th pct)")
ax.axhline(cut, color=CRASH, lw=0.9, ls="--", label=f"cutoff {cut:+.1%}")
ax.axhline(0, color=INK, lw=0.7)
ax.set_ylabel("average bank daily return"); ax.set_xlabel("date")
ax.set_title("The crash-day mask the labs reload", fontsize=12)
ax.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False, loc="lower left"); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
crash mask  q=10%  cutoff = -2.10%
  bank-average : 478 crash days (10.0% of 4778 days)
  JPM          : 478 crash days (10.0%)

first five flagged (bank-average) dates:
  2007-02-27   -4.70%
  2007-03-13   -3.17%
  2007-07-24   -3.04%
  2007-07-26   -2.75%
  2007-08-03   -3.22%
```
:::

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}

The bank-average return is plotted; days at or below its 10th percentile (the documented dial) are flagged with crash markers and the cutoff is drawn as a dashed line. This is the exact object the labs reload to split crash days from calm days — built once, here, with no re-derivation downstream.](03-crashes-and-drawdowns_files/figure-html/fig-reload-mask-output-2.png){#fig-reload-mask width=1088 height=441}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## The Lab Contract
The dependence labs **reload this crash mask** to compare crash-day vs calm-day
dependence — they do **not** re-derive it.  The mechanics (the loader, the percentile
dial, the boolean split) live *here*, in the data primer; the labs assume the recipe
above and climb straight to the metric.  The threshold (`q = 0.10`) is a **documented
dial**, not a magic constant: change it here and every consuming lab moves with it.

Consuming labs:

- [`dependence/labs/lab-tool1-ladder`](../dependence/labs/lab-tool1-ladder.qmd) — watches
  the distance-correlation−Spearman gap **open on crash days**, using this mask to split
  the sample.
- [`dependence/labs/lab-jobC-hidden-risk`](../dependence/labs/lab-jobC-hidden-risk.qmd) —
  measures **tail co-crash** on these flagged days to raise the portfolio risk flag.
:::

## Where This Goes Next

One name's crashes are dramatic; the real risk is that many names crash *together*.
→ [Co-Movement & Co-Crashes](04-co-movement-and-co-crashes.qmd).
